title: Hedging on the frontier: Learning new tasks with few samples
claim: A solution frontier can be covered by balls under a quasi-metric, with covering density adapting to the front's geometry.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared axes with dashed construction lines
description: Three side-by-side 2-D plots with axes R1 (horizontal) and R2 (vertical), each showing a convex decreasing Pareto curve. Panel (a), 'A Pareto ball', has a black curve with a red segment. The red segment is the points within distance t of a point r_j. Dashed lines and a gray diagonal labeled t1 link r_j to r_j − t1, and annotations read d(r_j, r) ≤ t. Panel (b), 'Two Pareto coverings', shows a steep orange curve and a straight blue line. Each is covered by labeled points (r1, r2, …, r6) joined by dashed staircase steps. The straight line needs more points than the curved one. Panel (c), 'Density from Theorem 1', shows a curve colored blue to red, with normal-vector arrows along it and a colorbar for density β(n) from 0 to 1. Density is highest where the normal is balanced and low where a normal component is small.
caption: Using the Pareto quasi-metric from Definition 5 to cover the Pareto front. In Fig. 2a the area covered by a single point rj (i.e., a Pareto ball). The number of points required adapts to the geometry of the front (2b). And in the limit, as t →0, the density of the covering β depends on the normal vector (2c), as specified in Theorem 1: If any of the coordinates nk of the normal vector n is small, the density is low.
abstract: When a learner faces a new task with few samples, it must leverage any available side information. In practice, this often comes in the form of model evaluations on related tasks in public benchmarks. A key question then is how to model task relatedness such that it is both realistic and the benchmark evaluations lead to provable gains. Empirically, we observe that weak monotonicity is often approximately satisfied: if a model dominates another on many benchmarks, it also tends to outperform on the new task. We explore the statistical complexity of learning under (approximate) weak monotonicity, leveraging it within two learning paradigms: transfer learning and model selection aggregation. We show that not only can we prune the model class based on monotonicity, but we can also further adapt to the geometry of the available trade-offs by hedging on the frontier.
